description: The Seljuk threat, Alexios's appeal, and Urban II's call to holy war at Clermont in 1095.
content_html:
The Seljuk Turks and the Threat to Byzantium

The catalyst for the First Crusade came from the east, where a new and powerful force had transformed the political map of the Middle East. The Seljuk Turks had swept out of Central Asia in the early eleventh century, converting to Sunni Islam and rapidly building an empire that stretched from Persia to Syria. In 1055 they entered Baghdad, making themselves protectors of the Abbasid caliph.

The decisive moment for the Byzantine Empire came at the Battle of Manzikert in 1071. A Byzantine army under Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes met the Seljuk forces of Sultan Alp Arslan in eastern Anatolia. The Byzantines suffered a catastrophic defeat: Romanos was captured, the Byzantine army was routed, and much of Anatolia — the heartland of Byzantine military manpower — fell under Seljuk control. By the 1090s the Seljuks were camped at Nicaea, barely 100 kilometres from Constantinople itself.

Key Fact

The Battle of Manzikert (1071) was a turning point in the origins of the Crusades. The Byzantine defeat opened Anatolia to Seljuk settlement, cutting off Byzantine military recruitment and threatening Constantinople. It created the crisis that prompted Emperor Alexios Komnenos to appeal to the West for help.

The Appeal of Alexios Komnenos

Alexios Komnenos became emperor in 1081 and proved a capable ruler, stabilising Byzantine finances and military power. But the Seljuk threat remained serious. In 1095, Alexios sent envoys to the Council of Piacenza, asking Pope Urban II for military mercenaries to help him recover Anatolia. Alexios wanted trained professional soldiers — knights who would fight under his command, recover land, and return home. What he got was something far bigger and far harder to control.

Why did Urban II respond so dramatically? The pope saw an opportunity to extend papal authority eastward, perhaps even to reunite the Eastern and Western Churches (which had formally split in 1054 in the Great Schism). A successful expedition would burnish papal prestige, redirect the violence of European knights from tearing apart Christian society, and fulfil the duty of protecting pilgrims to Jerusalem. Urban was thinking not just as a defender of Byzantium but as the leader of all Christendom.

The Council of Clermont, November 1095

In November 1095, Pope Urban II held a church council at Clermont in central France. On 27 November, at the end of the council, Urban addressed a large crowd gathered outside the city. His speech was a defining moment in medieval history. No verbatim record survives — accounts were written down years later by different chroniclers — but the sources agree on its key elements.

Urban described the sufferings of Eastern Christians under the Seljuks. He called on the knights of the West to stop fighting each other and turn their military skills toward a holy purpose. He urged them to march to Jerusalem and liberate the Holy Sepulchre, the site of Christ’s tomb, from Muslim rule. He promised that those who died on the journey would receive a plenary indulgence — full remission of all sins. According to chroniclers, the crowd responded with the cry Deus vult — “God wills it”.

Key Fact

Urban II’s offer of a plenary indulgence at Clermont was revolutionary. Medieval Christians believed that sins had to be expiated through penance in this life or suffering in purgatory after death. Full remission of all sins was an extraordinarily compelling promise, removing the greatest spiritual fear of a medieval person.

Historians debate whether religious devotion or material self-interest drove crusaders. Recent scholarship has emphasised genuine religious motivation: crusading was extremely expensive and dangerous, and most crusaders made a financial loss. However, individual motives were clearly mixed.

Religious motives included the desire for spiritual reward through the indulgence, a genuine devotion to the Holy Sepulchre, and the concept of pilgrimage-combined-with-warfare (the crusade was, legally and spiritually, a form of armed pilgrimage). Social and secular motives included the prospect of land and wealth in the East for younger sons who could not inherit at home, the desire for adventure and glory, and loyalty to lords who had taken the cross. For many, religion and self-interest were genuinely inseparable.

The Rise of Militant Christianity

The idea of a holy war did not emerge fully-formed at Clermont. It had roots in earlier papal campaigns. In the 1060s and 1070s, popes had granted spiritual rewards to knights fighting Muslim rulers in Spain and Sicily. The Cluniac reform movement had gradually created a Christian culture in which the concept of a “soldier of Christ” was not just metaphorical but potentially literal.

Urban II synthesised these ideas at Clermont. By framing the expedition as a holy pilgrimage — not merely a war — he gave crusaders both spiritual reward and a sense of moral legitimacy. Knights who worried that killing was sinful could now believe their swords served God. The response across France, Flanders, Lorraine, southern Italy and England was enormous: nobles, knights and even poor pilgrims began to take the cross.

Urban II intended his call to be directed at trained knights. But the response went far beyond the noble class. In spring 1096, a charismatic preacher named Peter the Hermit gathered a large following of poor pilgrims, minor knights and common people. This “People’s Crusade” set off months ahead of the official crusade army. Lacking supplies, discipline and military experience, Peter’s followers swept through Germany, massacring Jewish communities along the Rhine (the Rhineland Massacres of 1096) before crossing into Byzantine territory. The People’s Crusade was destroyed by the Seljuks in Anatolia in October 1096 before the main army had even left Europe.

The Rhineland Massacres — in which Jewish communities at Worms, Mainz and Cologne were attacked — revealed a dark consequence of the crusading ideology. The same militant Christianity that could be directed against Muslims in the East could also be turned violently against religious minorities at home. This connection between crusading and religious intolerance would recur throughout the era.
exam_tip_html: For questions on the causes of the First Crusade, you must connect the political context (Seljuk expansion, Byzantine appeal) with the ideological context (Cluniac reform, holy war, pilgrimage) and Urban II’s specific actions at Clermont. Examiners want you to weigh these factors — don’t just list them. For the 10-mark “Why do interpretations differ?” question type, be ready to explain why historians debate whether religious faith or material motives were more important for crusaders.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Battle of Manzikert (1071) opened Anatolia to the Seljuks and forced Emperor Alexios Komnenos to appeal to Rome for help, providing the immediate trigger for Urban II’s call to crusade.
  • At the Council of Clermont (November 1095), Urban II offered a plenary indulgence to all who took the cross — a revolutionary promise that made participation spiritually irresistible for medieval Christians.
  • Individual motives for crusading were mixed: genuine religious devotion, the lure of land and adventure, and loyalty to lords who had taken the cross all played a part.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Battle of Manzikert (1071).
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Students may describe: it was a Byzantine defeat against the Seljuk Turks; Emperor Romanos IV was captured; it opened Anatolia to Seljuk settlement; it threatened Constantinople. 1 mark for a simple point; 2 marks for a developed point with supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Pope Urban II's speech at the Council of Clermont in 1095.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should identify two features with supporting detail.
Feature 1: Urban II called on Western knights to stop fighting each other and march to liberate Jerusalem and the Holy Sepulchre from Muslim (Seljuk) control.
Feature 2: Urban II promised a plenary indulgence — full remission of all sins — to those who died on the expedition, an enormously powerful spiritual incentive.
2 marks per feature: 1 mark for a simple point, 2 marks for a developed point with supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the enormous popular response to Urban II's call for a crusade in 1095.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a specific cause and explains it with precise detail, linking it clearly to the scale of the response. E.g. the plenary indulgence addressed the deepest medieval spiritual fear (purgatory), making participation spiritually irresistible; or the tradition of Jerusalem pilgrimage meant crusaders saw themselves as armed pilgrims doing a holy duty. Sustains a clear line of reasoning.
Secure: Identifies a cause with some explanation and some link to outcome.
Developing: Identifies a cause but explanation is limited.
Emerging: Simple statement with little development.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Council of Clermont (1095) for the history of the Crusades.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Covers significance at the time (immediate surge in recruitment, nobles and peasants taking the cross, launch of both the People's Crusade and the official crusade) and over time (established papacy as organiser of holy war, set precedent for future crusades, fundamentally changed Western-Muslim relations). Sustained judgement throughout.
Secure: Covers both dimensions with evidence; clear explanation.
Developing: Mainly one dimension, limited evidence.
Emerging: Describes Clermont with little sense of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Seljuk conquest of Anatolia for the Byzantine Empire.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a specific consequence (e.g. loss of Anatolia removed the main source of Byzantine military recruits; Seljuks positioned at Nicaea threatened Constantinople; forced Alexios to appeal to the West, inadvertently starting the Crusades) and explains it with precise detail. Sustained reasoning.
Secure: Identifies a consequence with some explanation.
Developing: Identifies a consequence but explanation is limited.
Emerging: Simple statement with little development.

practice_questions.text: 'Religious devotion was the main reason why so many people responded to Urban II's call for a crusade.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues for (plenary indulgence addressed profound spiritual fear; pilgrimage tradition made Jerusalem sacred; growing ideology of holy war; many crusaders made financial sacrifice) and against (younger sons sought land and wealth; adventure and glory; loyalty to crusading lords; political ambitions of noble leaders). Reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Both sides argued with relevant evidence; conclusion reached.
Developing: Mainly one-sided, limited evidence.
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement.

knowledge_checks.q: In which year did the Battle of Manzikert take place?
What did Pope Urban II promise to crusaders who died on the expedition?
options: A grant of land in the Holy Land
Exemption from all taxes for their families
A plenary indulgence — full remission of all sins

knowledge_checks.q: Emperor _____ Komnenos sent envoys to Pope Urban II asking for Western military help against the Seljuks.
According to chroniclers, the crowd at Clermont responded to Urban's speech with the cry _____, meaning 'God wills it'.
Match each event with its correct date.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Battle of Manzikert?
Who captured the Byzantine Emperor at Manzikert?
What territory did the Seljuks control after Manzikert that threatened Constantinople?
Which Byzantine emperor appealed to Pope Urban II for military help?
When and where did Urban II make his call for a crusade?
flashcard_questions.a: November 1095, at the Council of Clermont.

flashcard_questions.q: A plenary indulgence in medieval theology meant what?
flashcard_questions.a: Full remission of all sins, reducing time in purgatory.

flashcard_questions.q: What phrase did the crowd at Clermont reportedly cry out in response to Urban II?
Who led the People's Crusade in 1096?
What happened to the People's Crusade in October 1096?
flashcard_questions.a: It was destroyed by the Seljuks in Anatolia.

flashcard_questions.q: The Rhineland Massacres of 1096 targeted which religious community?
flashcard_questions.a: Jewish communities in German Rhineland cities.

flashcard_questions.q: What formal split between Eastern and Western Christianity occurred in 1054?
Why did Urban II direct his call at knights specifically?
flashcard_questions.a: To redirect their military violence from tearing apart Christian society toward a holy cause.

glossary_terms.definition: A Turkic Muslim dynasty that rose to power in the eleventh century, defeating Byzantium at Manzikert in 1071 and controlling much of Anatolia and the Holy Land.
Byzantine Emperor (r. 1081–1118) who appealed to Pope Urban II for Western military aid against the Seljuk Turks, helping to trigger the First Crusade.
In medieval Catholic theology, a reduction in the time a soul would spend in purgatory, granted by the Pope in exchange for a specific religious act.
The concept that warfare could be spiritually meritorious when waged in defence of Christianity or to recover holy sites, developed by the papacy in the eleventh century.
